questions.title: Positioning a smaller rival
questions.prompt: You are the product marketer for a new expense-management tool competing with two large, well-known products. Your product is simpler and cheaper but has fewer integrations. Position it.
hints: Which customers are badly served by the big products?
What do those customers use today instead?
What can you credibly claim, with proof?
followups: Sales says every deal is lost on integrations. Does that change your positioning?
How would you test the positioning before a full launch?
A large competitor launches a 'lite' plan. Respond.
criteria: Identifies a best-fit segment underserved by incumbents.
Names the real alternatives, including spreadsheets.
Turns unique attributes into value with proof.
Chooses a market frame that makes the strengths matter.
Tests positioning with customers and sales.
outline: Best fit: companies of 10–100 employees without a finance team, using spreadsheets or card statements.
Alternatives: spreadsheets, bank exports, heavy enterprise tools.
Unique: setup in a day, no implementation, transparent price.
Value: expenses done without a finance team.
Frame: 'expense management for teams without a finance department'.
Proof: setup time, customer quotes.
Test: win/loss, message tests, sales feedback.
questions.reference:
I would not position against the big products head-on; they win on breadth. The best-fit customer is a company of roughly 10 to 100 people without a finance department, using spreadsheets and card statements today. For them, the big tools are too heavy: weeks to implement, priced for larger firms.

Positioning: “Expense management for teams without a finance department — set up in a day, no implementation, one transparent price.” The real alternative is the spreadsheet, so the message is about time saved and fewer errors, not about out-featuring incumbents. Proof: median setup time, customer quotes, a live demo of a month-end close.

Integrations matter to larger customers, so losing those deals may mean sales is chasing the wrong segment. I would check win/loss by company size. Before a full launch I would test the message with ads and sales calls. If a competitor launches a lite plan, our answer is simplicity they cannot match without rebuilding.

questions.title: Three audiences, one feature
questions.prompt: Your company is launching single sign-on and audit logs for its collaboration software. Write the message hierarchy for three audiences: the IT buyer, the end user and the security reviewer.
hints: What does each audience worry about?
What stays the same across all three?
followups: The end users do not care at all. Should you message them?
How would you test the IT message?
criteria: One core message with audience-specific pillars.
Grounded in each audience's concern.
Specific proof (standards, certifications, controls) without overclaiming.
Plain language.
Plan to test.
outline: Core: 'enterprise-grade control without slowing teams down'.
IT buyer: central control, faster onboarding/offboarding, fewer tickets; proof: supported identity providers, setup time.
End user: one login, nothing new to learn.
Security reviewer: audit trail coverage, retention, export; certifications.
Avoid: 'unhackable', unverified compliance claims.
questions.reference:
Core message for everyone: “Enterprise-grade control, without slowing your teams down.”

IT buyer: they worry about access when people join and leave, and about support tickets. Pillars: manage access centrally through your identity provider; remove a leaver’s access everywhere in one step; fewer password-reset tickets. Proof: the identity providers supported and typical setup time.

End user: they want nothing to change. Message: “Sign in with your work account — one less password.” Short, in-product, at the moment it matters.

Security reviewer: they want evidence. Pillars: what events the audit log records, how long it keeps them, how to export to their security tools, and our certifications. Proof: documentation and a sample log. I would avoid absolute claims such as ‘completely secure’ or compliance statements we have not verified. I would test the IT message in sales calls and an ad test before launch.

questions.title: Launching an AI add-on
questions.prompt: Your company is launching a paid AI add-on for its customer-support software in eight weeks. Build the go-to-market plan.
hints: What must sales and support know on day one?
How will you measure the launch beyond press?
followups: The product team says quality may not be ready for all languages. What changes?
Sales wants a big discount to drive adoption. Your view?
What does week one after launch look like?
criteria: Sets goals and launch tier.
Defines target segments and sequencing (beta customers, existing base, new market).
Prepares sales, support and partners before announcement.
Plans channels and proof (customer stories, ROI).
Defines launch metrics and post-launch iteration.
outline: Goals: pipeline, attach rate, activation of purchased add-ons.
Segments: existing customers with high ticket volume first.
Proof: beta customer results with permission; ROI calculator; honest limits.
Readiness: sales training, pricing, objection handling, support documentation.
Channels: in-product, customer success outreach, webinar, announcement.
Metrics: pipeline created, attach rate, time to first value, churn of add-on.
Week one: monitor activation and feedback; fix messaging.
questions.reference:
Goals first: pipeline created, attach rate among existing customers, and — most important for an AI product — activation: buyers who actually turn it on and see value.

Segments: existing customers with high ticket volume first, because the value is easiest to prove and they already trust us. The proof comes from beta customers who agree to share results, an ROI calculator, and an honest statement of what the AI does not do yet — for example, languages not yet supported.

Readiness two weeks before announcement: sales trained on the pitch, pricing and objections; support documentation and a playbook; partners briefed. Channels: in-product messages to admins, customer-success outreach to target accounts, a webinar with beta customers, then the public announcement.

On discounts, I would rather offer a time-limited trial than a permanent discount; it proves value without anchoring a low price. Week one: daily review of activation, support tickets and sales feedback, with messaging adjusted quickly.

questions.title: Why we lose
questions.prompt: Your company's win rate against one competitor has fallen from about one in two deals to about one in three over two quarters. Design the research to find out why.
hints: Who knows why a deal was lost — and who will tell you the truth?
How do you avoid only hearing sales' explanation?
Which deal data would you look at first?
followups: Sales says it is price. Interviews say it is onboarding. What do you do?
How do you turn findings into action?
criteria: Combines deal data with buyer interviews (win and loss).
Uses a neutral interviewer and structured guide.
Segments by deal size, industry, region.
Separates stated reasons from underlying ones.
Turns findings into specific actions with owners.
outline: Data: win rate by segment, stage of loss, deal size, discount.
Interviews: recent wins and losses, buyer side, neutral interviewer.
Guide: decision process, criteria, alternatives, moment of choice.
Synthesis: themes by frequency and deal value.
Actions: product, pricing, messaging, sales process; owners and dates.
questions.reference:
I would start with deal data: win rate by segment, deal size, region and the stage at which deals are lost. If losses concentrate in one segment or stage, that focuses the interviews.

Then talk to buyers — both wins and losses from the last two quarters — using a neutral interviewer (someone not from the sales team) and a structured guide: how they decided, who was involved, what criteria mattered, when the choice was really made. Buyers often tell sales ‘price’ because it is easy; the interviews reveal underlying reasons such as onboarding effort or a missing integration.

Twenty or so interviews usually show the main themes; I would continue until new interviews stop adding themes. Findings are weighted by deal value and turned into actions with owners: a product gap to product, a pricing structure issue to pricing, a message problem to us, a sales-process issue to sales leadership.

questions.title: Is product marketing working?
questions.prompt: Your new CMO asks how they should judge whether product marketing is working. What do you propose?
hints: What does product marketing influence directly?
How do you avoid taking credit for everything or nothing?
What leading indicators exist before revenue?
followups: Attribution says marketing drove 90% of pipeline. Do you believe it?
Which metric would you drop after a year?
criteria: Ties to revenue outcomes (pipeline, win rate, attach rate) while being honest about attribution.
Includes leading indicators (message tests, launch adoption).
Measures enablement use and effect.
Uses win/loss as a recurring input.
Avoids vanity metrics.
outline: Outcomes: win rate in target segments, launch adoption, attach rate, pipeline in target segments.
Leading: message test results, content used in deals.
Enablement: training completion, asset use, rep confidence, win rate change.
Win/loss: quarterly themes and actions.
Attribution: use ranges; avoid last-touch claims.
questions.reference:
I would propose a small set of outcomes product marketing clearly influences: win rate against key competitors, adoption of launched features, attach rate of add-ons, and pipeline in the segments we target. Leading indicators help earlier: how messages perform in tests, and which content sales actually uses in deals that are won.

For enablement, the measure is not training completion but whether reps use the material and win rates change for those who do. A quarterly win/loss review keeps everyone honest about why deals are won and lost.

On attribution, I would be cautious: claims that marketing drove 90% of pipeline usually come from models that credit any touch. I would report ranges and focus on comparisons we can trust — for example, win rates before and after a positioning change.

questions.title: Product and sales disagreed
questions.prompt: Tell me about a time product and sales wanted different things from a launch and you were in the middle.
hints: What did each side want and why?
What did you do to resolve it?
followups: How did it affect your relationships?
criteria: Represents both sides fairly.
Uses customer evidence to resolve.
Finds a solution both can support.
Clear outcome.
Lesson.
outline: Situation.
Each side's position.
Your approach and evidence.
Resolution.
Outcome.
Lesson.
questions.reference: A strong answer (a model of structure, not a script): “Product wanted to launch a new analytics feature as a free upgrade; sales wanted it in the premium tier to justify a price rise. I ran ten customer calls and found that basic reports were expected by everyone, but scheduled exports were what larger customers would pay for. We launched basic reports free and exports in premium. Premium upgrades rose that quarter and product got adoption. I learned to bring customers into the room rather than mediate opinions.”
